sections.text:
Someone is preaching to a tired and pressured people, and he cannot name everyone he wants to name. In the middle of a long roll call of men and women who lived by faith, he stops. “the time would fail me” if he told of them all. This is Hebrews, and it reads less like a letter than like a sermon.

Its argument is built step by step. Jesus is greater than the angels. He is greater than Moses. He is greater than the priests of the old covenant, because he is the high priest who offered himself once for all, and now gives free access to God.

Between the arguments come warnings not to drift away, and encouragements to hold on. In chapter 11 comes the definition the writer sets before his readers: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen”, and the chapter fills it with lives. Then the call goes out to run with endurance, “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith”.

No name stands at the head of this sermon, and the author is unknown. Paul was named in the eastern churches from early on, and Barnabas and Apollos have also been suggested. The readers seem to be Jewish Christians tempted to give up under pressure. Many scholars date it before the year 70, since it speaks of sacrifices as still being offered.

The warnings, especially 6:4 to 6 and 10:26 to 31, are read differently. Some conclude that a true believer can fall away. Others hold that the warnings describe people who belonged to the community without true faith, or that they are the means God uses to keep believers going. These are old and serious conversations among Christians, and each side takes the warnings seriously, since the writer himself plainly does.

The letter begins without a greeting and without a name. It begins with God speaking. God spoke to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in many ways, but at the end of these days he has spoken through his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things and through whom he made the worlds. The Son is “the radiance of his glory,” upholds all things by his word, and after purifying us from sins sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.

The rest of the chapter argues that he is greater than the angels. The writer strings together lines of Scripture: you are my Son, let all the angels of God worship him, your throne, O God, is forever. Angels are winds and flames of fire, but the Son is addressed as God and Lord, who laid the foundation of the earth and remains when it grows old. The chapter ends by calling the angels serving spirits, sent to help those who will inherit salvation.

Hebrews is an anonymous sermon in the form of a letter. Some churches long held it as Paul’s, but many scholars think its author is unknown. It is usually dated to the first century, and some think before AD 70, since it speaks of temple worship in the present tense. Its readers seem to be Jewish Christians under pressure. The quotations in this chapter come from Psalm 2, 2 Samuel 7, Psalm 45, Psalm 102 and Psalm 110. Christians read verse 8 as calling the Son God.

After the grand claim of chapter 1, the writer gives a warning with a gentle edge: pay closer attention to what you have heard, “lest perhaps we drift away.” If the word spoken through angels held firm, how could anyone escape if they neglect so great a salvation?

Then the writer turns to the Psalms and asks what humanity is, that God should think of them. Humanity was made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honor, yet we do not yet see everything under its feet. What we do see is Jesus, made a little lower than the angels for a time, crowned with glory and honor because he suffered death, so that by the grace of God he would taste death for everyone.

He shared flesh and blood to bring to nothing the one who had the power of death, and to free those who lived in lifelong fear of it. He was made like his brothers, a merciful and faithful high priest, and “he is able to help those who are tempted.”

The warning in the first verses follows directly from the argument that the Son is greater than the angels. The writer quotes Psalm 8, which asks what a human being is, and reads it as fulfilled in Jesus. Christians have read the passage about the one who had the power of death in different ways, as a defeat of the devil, of death itself, or both. The audience seems to be Jewish Christians facing hardship, and the author is unknown. See Psalm 22 and Isaiah 8 for the other quotations.

The writer asks his readers to look closely at Jesus, the apostle and high priest of their confession. Jesus was faithful to the one who appointed him, as Moses was faithful in all God’s house. But Jesus is counted worthy of more glory, as the builder of a house has more honor than the house. Moses was faithful as a servant, but Christ is faithful as a Son over his house, and “We are his house, if we hold fast our confidence”.

Then the writer turns to Psalm 95 and the story of the wilderness. “Today if you will hear his voice, don’t harden your hearts”. The fathers tested God for forty years even though they saw his works, and God swore that they would not enter his rest. The writer asks who it was that rebelled, and answers that it was all those who came out of Egypt under Moses. They could not enter because of unbelief.

So the readers are to encourage one another day by day, as long as it is called today, so that none is hardened.

The writer sets Jesus beside Moses, the most honored figure in Israel’s history, to show that Jesus is greater and that his readers should stay faithful. The wilderness story is told in Numbers 14, and the psalm is Psalm 95. Christians differ on what the condition if we hold fast means. Some say it describes the mark of true believers, others that believers can fall away. The author is unknown, and the letter is usually dated to the first century.

The writer keeps pressing on the word rest. The good news was preached to the people in the wilderness as well, but it did not help them because it was not joined with faith. Yet God’s rest still stands open. The seventh day, when God rested from his works, is a sign of it, and the psalm says again through David, long after Joshua, “Today if you will hear his voice”. So a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and the readers are urged to make every effort to enter it.

The word of God, the writer says, is “living and active,” sharper than a two-edged sword, and nothing is hidden from the one to whom we must give account.

The chapter ends with a gift. We have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, who was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. So let us come boldly to the throne of grace, to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

The argument builds on Genesis 2, where God rests on the seventh day, on Psalm 95, and on the story of Joshua’s generation entering the land in Joshua. Christians differ on how to read the rest: as salvation received now, as the life to come, or as a Sabbath practice, and often as a mix of these. The author is unknown, and the letter is usually dated to the first century. The mention of Jesus as high priest prepares the chapters that follow.

The writer describes what a high priest is. He is taken from among people and appointed to act for them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins. Because he is surrounded by weakness himself, he can deal gently with the ignorant and those who go astray. No one takes this honor for himself, and he must be called by God, as Aaron was.

Christ did not glorify himself to be made high priest either. God said to him, You are my Son, and in another place, you are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. In the days of his flesh he offered prayers and petitions “with strong crying and tears”, and though he was a Son, he learned obedience by what he suffered. Having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him.

Then the writer stops short, and rebukes his readers. There is much to say about Melchizedek, but they have become dull of hearing. They should be teachers, yet they need someone to teach them again, for they “need milk, and not solid food.”

The author sets out to show that Jesus is a priest of a different kind from Aaron’s line, using Psalm 2 and Psalm 110. Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14 and is taken up fully in the next chapters. The sharp rebuke to the readers shows that this is a pastoral letter to a community in danger of settling for less. The author is unknown, and the letter is usually dated to the first century. Christians have read the line about being made perfect in different ways.

The writer says it is time to leave the first lessons and press on to maturity. He does not want to lay the foundation again: repentance, faith in God, teaching about washings, laying on of hands, resurrection and judgment.

Then a sobering passage. It is impossible to renew to repentance those who were once enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, and then fell away, since they crucify the Son of God again and hold him up to shame. A field that drinks the rain and bears a crop is blessed, but one that bears thorns and thistles is near to being cursed.

At once the writer softens. He is “persuaded of better things” for them. God is not unjust and will not forget their work and love. He wants them to hold on to the end and to imitate those who inherited the promises. God swore by himself to Abraham, and the oath gives a strong encouragement, an anchor for the soul, entering behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone before us as a forerunner and high priest forever.

Verses 4 to 6 are among the most debated in the Bible. Christians read them in several ways. Some think they describe true believers who can lose salvation. Others think they describe people who seemed to belong but never truly did. Others read them as a warning meant to keep believers from falling. The writer’s own next lines show his confidence in his readers. The promise to Abraham is told in Genesis 22. The author is unknown, and the letter is usually dated to the first century.

Melchizedek is a mysterious figure who appears briefly in the Bible, and the writer now makes him the key. He was king of Salem and priest of God Most High, and he met Abraham coming back from battle and blessed him. Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. His name means king of righteousness, and king of Salem means king of peace. He is described without father, mother or genealogy, with neither beginning of days nor end of life, made like the Son of God.

The writer reasons that the lesser is blessed by the greater, so Melchizedek is greater than Abraham and even than Levi, from whom the priests came. If the Levitical priesthood had been enough, why would another priest be needed? Jesus comes from the tribe of Judah and is a priest by the power of an indestructible life, with an oath: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Because he lives forever, he is “able to save to the uttermost” those who draw near to God through him, and he offered himself once for all.

Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14 and in Psalm 110, and the writer builds on these two short passages. The letter speaks of the old law as weak and useless, and these words have been misused to look down on Judaism. The writer is arguing within a Jewish setting about what the priesthood could not finish. Christians differ on how the old and new covenants relate. The author is unknown, and the letter is usually dated to the first century.

Here is the main point, says the writer: we have a high priest who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, a servant of the true tabernacle that the Lord set up, not man. The priests on earth serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things. That is why Moses was warned to make everything according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain.

But Jesus has a more excellent ministry, as mediator of a better covenant resting on better promises. If the first had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second. So the writer quotes the long promise of Jeremiah. The days are coming, says the Lord, when he will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. “I will put my laws into their mind; I will also write them on their heart.” All will know him, and he will remember their sins no more.

By calling it new, he has made the first obsolete, and what is old is near to vanishing.

The writer quotes Jeremiah 31 at length. The tabernacle pattern is from Exodus 25. The word obsolete has been misused to claim that God has set Israel aside, and Christians differ on how the new covenant relates to the Jewish people. Many hold that the promise was made to Israel and that Gentiles share in it. The author is unknown, and the letter is usually dated to the first century.

The writer walks his readers through the tent where Israel worshiped. In the first room stood the lampstand, the table and the bread. Behind the second curtain was the Holy of Holies, with the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant, which held the jar of manna, Aaron’s rod that budded and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory. The priests entered the first room continually, but into the second went only the high priest, once a year, and never without blood.

Christ came as high priest of the good things to come. He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, once for all, having obtained “eternal redemption.” How much more can the blood of Christ cleanse the conscience?

The writer recalls how Moses sprinkled the covenant with blood and says that “apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.” Christ appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin by his sacrifice, and will appear a second time to save those waiting for him.

The writer draws on the tabernacle laws of Leviticus 16 and the covenant ceremony in Exodus 24. The sacrificial language is difficult for many modern readers, and Christians have understood Christ’s death in several ways, with different pictures of how it takes away sin. The author plays on the idea of a will, which takes effect at a death. The author is unknown, and the letter is usually dated to the first century, with some placing it before the temple was destroyed in AD 70.
